summary: The English of Genesis 3:8–15 is faithful and plain throughout. It follows Rashi and Ibn Ezra where they agree, and it records the readings where they differ (רוּחַ הַיּוֹם, the verb שׁוּף, גָּחוֹן). The faults are in the apparatus. The man in 3:8–12 was given BDB's collective sense of אָדָם. A figurative sense was chosen for תֵלֵךְ, and כֹּל lacks its sense. Several learner notes are false: they call the ה of אַיֶּכָּה pausal, call עָשִׂית an 'old' 2fs, give the rule for the doubled pashta the wrong way round, and let a 1cp parse of מִמֶּנּוּ pass without a note. Three commentary summaries misstate their comments: Rashi on מִכָּל הַבְּהֵמָה, and Ibn Ezra on עִמָּדִי and on וָאֹכֵל. The translator's note on 3:12 also misreports Ibn Ezra and Ramban.

patches.reason: הָאָדָם here is the one man with his wife: BDB sense 1, 'a man = human being'. Sense 2 is the collective 'man, mankind'.
As at 3:8.11: the individual man, BDB sense 1, not the collective sense 2.

patches.value: אַיֶּכָּה is אַי 'where' with the 2ms suffix in its full spelling ־כָה (= ־ךָ); the copula is not written
patches.reason: The ה is not caused by the pause. ־כָה is the full (plene) spelling of the 2ms suffix ־ךָ, and it is found outside pause too.

value: וַיִּקְרָא ... אֶל, 'call to', takes אֶל for the one called.
אַיֶּכָּה: אַי 'where?' with the 2ms suffix written in full, ־כָה for ־ךָ; the ה is a spelling of the suffix, not a pausal change. The sentence has no verb: 'where-you?'.
The etnaḥta on הָאָדָם divides the verse: the call, then the question.
patches.reason: The second note called the ה of ־כָה a pausal spelling. It is the full spelling of the 2ms suffix.

value: אֶת־קֹלְךָ שָׁמַעְתִּי: the object is fronted before the verb, so that the sound is what is stressed.
קוֹל is rendered 'sound', not 'voice': Genesis 3:8 has the same word of the LORD God walking.
וָאִירָא and וָאֵחָבֵא are wayyiqtol forms in the first person, with ָ on the ו; the second verb is niphal (reflexive).
עֵירֹם, 'naked', is written with a yod (cf. 3:11). עֵירֹם אָנֹכִי is a verbless clause: the predicate comes first and the pronoun אָנֹכִי is its subject, 'I am naked'.
patches.reason: אָנֹכִי is not added for emphasis. In a verbless clause the pronoun is the subject itself and cannot be left out.

patches.value: מִמֶּנּוּ 'from it', that is, from the tree; the pack's data parse the suffix as 1st person plural ('from us'), a form identical to the 3ms, but the antecedent הָעֵץ requires the 3ms
patches.reason: The morphology in the pack gives the suffix as 1cp. The gloss 'from it' is right but contradicts that data, and translate rule 2 asks for the disagreement to be stated in a note.
The individual man speaking: BDB sense 1, not the collective sense 2.

patches.value: independent pronoun resuming 'the woman' after the casus pendens; written הוא in the Torah and pointed הִוא, it is read as the feminine 'she' (the Pentateuch's regular spelling of the 3fs pronoun)
patches.reason: A learner needs to know why a pronoun spelled הוא is read 'she'. The pack's parse is feminine.

patches.value: wayyiqtol 1cs, in pause: tsere in אֹכֵל for the patah of the usual וָאֹכַל; Ibn Ezra explains the form
patches.reason: The note should name the pausal form at silluq.

patches.value: נָתַתָּה is written with a final ה, a 2ms perfect in its full spelling. Ibn Ezra glosses the clause 'you gave (me) the one who gave to me'. 'Put' for נתן follows BDB's 'put, set'. Rashi (with the rabbis, Avodah Zarah 5) hears ingratitude in the line, as if the man blamed God for the gift. Ramban reads it as the man's plea: he took the woman God had given as a help, and thought her counsel would help him. Ramban then records the rabbis' reading.
patches.reason: The old note gave Ibn Ezra's gloss as 'you who gave me the woman who is with me'; his words are אתה נתת הנותנת לי, 'you gave the one who gave to me'. It also put Ramban with Rashi in seeing blame laid on God. Ramban's own reading is a plea, and he only records the rabbis' charge of ingratitude.

patches.value: Ibn Ezra: 'you gave the one who gave to me' (אתה נתת הנותנת לי). עִמָּדִי means 'with me in the garden' and is the same as עִמִּי, but the form is found only with the first-person singular suffix (לשון יחיד המדבר).
patches.reason: 'Not found except in the speech of one person' misreads לשון יחיד המדבר. The term is grammatical: the form עִמָּד occurs only with the 1cs suffix.

patches.value: Ibn Ezra on וָאֹכֵל: the א is the sign of the first person, and the quiescent letter after it stands for the root's א. The last syllable has 'small qamets' (tsere: אֹכֵל, not אֹכַל) because the word ends the verse. He adds that a ו with qamets does not otherwise come with the verb, 'for it is always with sheva'.
patches.reason: The old summary put the pausal vowel under the ו. Ibn Ezra's קמץ קטן (tsere) is the vowel of the final syllable, אֹכֵל, which is lengthened at the end of the verse.

patches.value: perfect 2fs; in a III-ה verb the 2fs ends in ־ִית (עָשִׂית), against the 2ms עָשִׂיתָ of 3:14
patches.reason: עָשִׂית is the ordinary 2fs perfect of a III-ה verb, not an 'old 2fs' (the archaic 2fs is the ־תִּי of the ketiv in a few places).

patches.value: wayyiqtol 1cs, in pause (tsere for the usual patah), as in 3:12
patches.reason: Name the pausal form for the learner.

value: מַה־זֹּאת עָשִׂית: 'what is this that you did?'; the 2fs perfect of a III-ה verb ends in ־ית.
The wayyiqtol וַתֹּאמֶר carries pashta twice. Pashta is written on the last letter, so a word stressed before its last syllable repeats it on the stressed syllable: וַתֹּ֙אמֶר֙, stress on תֹּ.
הַנָּחָשׁ הִשִּׁיאַנִי: subject first and the verb after it, the order of an answer.
הִשִּׁיאַנִי is a hifil of נשׁא with the suffix; the sense is 'to deceive' (BDB 'beguile'), not the common 'lift'.
The woman repeats the man's וָאֹכֵל: 'and I ate'.
patches.reason: The second note had the rule the wrong way round. Pashta is doubled when the stress is not on the last syllable.
כֹּל before a genitive is BDB sense 1, 'the whole of, any, every'. The entry lists senses, so a noun needs one.
As at 3:14.11: כֹּל with a following genitive, sense 1.

Qal II.2 is the figurative 'live (walk)', of moral and religious life, and II.1 is 'pass away, die'. The literal 'go, walk' that the serpent's going on its belly needs is not among the senses the pack lists, so the sense is removed.

patches.value: yiqtol 2ms of הלך, formed as from ילך (the lemma is given as יָלַךְ); the entry in the pack lists no literal Qal sense 'go, walk', only the figurative 'die' and 'live', so no sense is cited
patches.reason: Gives the reason the sense was removed, as the review brief requires.

value: The segolta on זֹּאת closes the first part of the half-verse before the etnaḥta: 'The LORD God said to the serpent, because you have done this'. Unlike the man and the woman, the serpent is not questioned (Rashi, Radak).
אָרוּר אַתָּה: a passive participle with a pronoun, as a curse; no copula.
מִכָּל הַבְּהֵמָה: מִן can be comparative ('more than') or partitive ('from among'); the English takes the first.
עַל־גְּחֹנְךָ תֵלֵךְ: the phrase comes before the verb, which puts the stress on 'belly'; תֵלֵךְ is a yiqtol of הלך.
וְעָפָר תֹּאכַל: the object is fronted again, so that the two curses balance, 'on belly ... and dust ...'.
כָּל־יְמֵי חַיֶּיךָ: an idiom for 'as long as you live'; חַיִּים is a plural noun.
patches.reason: The first note did not name the dividing accent (segolta on זֹּאת). It also tied the point that the serpent is not questioned to the accents; that point comes from the commentators.

patches.value: Rashi: if it was cursed more than the livestock, then all the more so more than the wild animals. The rabbis (Bekhorot 8) used the verse to teach that the serpent's gestation is seven years. The English takes מִן as 'more than'.
patches.reason: Rashi's אִם מִבְּהֵמָה נִתְקַלֵּל מֵחַיָּה לֹא כָּל שֶׁכֵּן is comparative: cattle are cursed more than wild animals, so a curse beyond the cattle is beyond the wild animals too. The gestation teaching in Bekhorot rests on that reading. 'Cursed from among' turns the reading the English follows into the partitive one it rejects.
Rashi takes יְשׁוּפְךָ as יְכַתֶּתְךָ, 'crush you'. The English 'strike' follows Ibn Ezra's יככה and Radak's מכה, and the summary itself says that Rashi's 'crush' is recorded in the note.

verdicts.comment: Rashi's statement of method; it does not bear on the words.
The thing heard is the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden.

Rashi takes רוּחַ as a direction (the west, at evening), and Ibn Ezra as the wind blowing toward evening. They agree on the hour but differ on the word. The English follows Ibn Ezra's 'breeze' and records Rashi's reading, as the translate rules allow; it stands.
'The sound ... walking about' keeps Ibn Ezra's reading, in which the sound goes.
The plain question stands; its purpose is in the note.
Rendered as a question.
'not to eat': לבלתי with ל = שלא.
Rashi gives a moral judgment on the man's words; the English keeps the words without adding the judgment.
'with me' for עִמָּדִי.
A grammatical comment on the form; the summary has been corrected.
'deceived' = הִטְעַנִי.
'deceived' fits פתני.
A halakhic inference (no plea is made for the inciter).
Comparative 'more than', as Rashi reads it; the summary has been corrected.
Rashi's legs that were cut off are midrash beyond the words; 'on your belly you shall go' does not conflict with it.
The English leaves the curse unexplained; Ibn Ezra's 'deficient in its going' matches the next clause.

Ibn Ezra glosses גחון as החזה, 'the chest'; the English has 'belly' with BDB, Onkelos (מְעָךְ) and Radak. Rashi does not comment, so the normative commentators do not agree against the English. 'Chest' is recorded in the apparatus, and the English stands.
'Strike' covers Rashi's 'crush', which is recorded in the note; the relation is corrected to records.
Rashi notes that the same word is used in both clauses for the wordplay; the English keeps 'strike' twice.
'on the head' supplies the missing ב, as Ibn Ezra says.
